lessons.title: 我 (wǒ) — seven strokes, and an honest admission
lessons.gloss: seven strokes, and none of them a piece you already own

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — the shape and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Write 是. Nine strokes, sun finished on top.
我 (wǒ).
Seven strokes, and here this book owes you a straight answer.

Every character so far has come apart into pieces you already had: 你 into 亻 and 尔, 是 into 日 and a body, 早 into 日 and 十. 我 (wǒ) does not. Its right side is a shape called 戈 — there it is, but naming it is all this lesson will do with it, because you have not been taught to write it. Its left side is a squeezed hand. Neither is a piece you own.
So learn it as a route, not as a sum. Follow the order and it holds together:
a short falling stroke at the upper left.
the upper horizontal, left to right.
the vertical, coming down and hooking left without lifting.
the lower rising stroke.
the long curved slash down to the right, hooking upward at its end.
a separate rising slash up to the left.
a dot at the upper right, pressed down-right.
Six pen lifts.

Two of these are joined strokes that must not be broken: stroke 3 (down, then hook) and stroke 5 (the long slash, then hook up). Everything you have learned about turning strokes applies here — the pen changes direction, the stroke does not end.
The dot goes last. Small marks at the upper right are finishers, and you will see that again.

segments.instruction: 我 (wǒ) slowly, twice — and keep strokes 3 and 5 unbroken
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: 我 slowly, twice — and keep strokes 3 and 5 unbroken]

segments.instruction: 我 (wǒ) once more, saving the dot for last
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: 我 once more, saving the dot for last]
[YOU SAY: **wǒ** — low and dipping]

segments.text: Is this character built from pieces you already know? (No — and this book would rather say so than invent a story.)
Source: Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart; stroke order per the PRC standard Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan (1997).

segments.prompt: Which stroke of this seven-stroke character is written last?

feedback.correct: The dot at the upper right -- small finishing marks come last.
feedback.incorrect: The DOT at the upper right.

lessons.title: 我 (wǒ) — I, me, and saying who you are
lessons.gloss: I, me — one word for both, and no change for either

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Say wǒ. Low and dipping, and hold the bottom of it.
我 wǒ — I. And also me.

English uses two words there and swaps between them depending on the job: I saw her, she saw me. Mandarin uses 我 (wǒ) for both, and this is your first sight of something that will save you a great deal of work: Mandarin words do not change shape for grammar. No endings, no cases, no agreement. 我 (wǒ) is 我 (wǒ) wherever it stands.
Now put it to work with a word you already have:
我是 wǒ shì — I am.
是 is the word you learned for answering yes. Its actual job is to link two things: 我是 (wǒ shì) and then who you are. Say your own name after it and you have introduced yourself.
Two third tones meet in wǒ shì? No — 是 is fourth tone. Nothing moves.

segments.instruction: wǒ, then wǒ shì — low and dipping, then falling
segments.source: [YOU SAY: **wǒ**, then **wǒ shì** — low and dipping, then falling]

segments.instruction: wǒ shì followed by your own name, out loud, twice
segments.source: [YOU SAY: **wǒ shì** followed by your own name, out loud, twice]
[YOU WRITE: 我是]

segments.text: What does 是 do in 我是 (wǒ shì)? (It links you to whatever comes next.)
Source: Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart.

segments.prompt: English has two words, 'I' and 'me', and picks between them. How many does Mandarin use?

feedback.correct: One -- 我 does both jobs, because the word never changes shape.
feedback.incorrect: ONE. 我 covers both, since Mandarin words do not change for grammar.

lessons.title: 名 (míng) — a mouth with something above it
lessons.gloss: six strokes, and the mouth you already know sits underneath

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — the shape and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Write 口. Three strokes, and the box is not closed until the last one.
名 (míng).
Six strokes, and three of them are 口, which you already own.
名 (míng) is 夕 sitting on top of 口. The lower half is the mouth. The upper half is 夕, a shape this book has not taught you as a character of its own — here it is a piece, and naming it is enough:
夕's upper falling stroke, down to the left.
夕's horizontal, continuing down-left without lifting — one stroke.
夕's inner dot, pressed down-right 4-6. 口, complete. Left side; top and right in one turning stroke; the bottom bar closing it.
Five pen lifts.

Finish 夕 before you begin 口 — the same instinct as finishing 日 before the body of 是, and finishing the sun before 十 in 早. You have now met that rule often enough that it should feel like the obvious thing to do.

A hook worth having, offered as a hook: 夕 is the shape used for evening, and a mouth beneath it reads easily as speaking your name in the dark, when you cannot be seen. That is a traditional story, not proven history — but 名 (míng) does mean name, and the picture makes the character stick.

segments.instruction: 口 alone, then 名 (míng) — and notice the last three strokes are identical
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: 口 alone, then 名 — and notice the last three strokes are identical]
[YOU WRITE: 名 again, keeping stroke 2 unbroken]
[YOU SAY: **míng** — rising]

segments.text: Which half goes first? (The top — as always.)
Source: Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart; stroke order per the PRC standard Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan (1997).

segments.prompt: Which character that you have already written forms the bottom half of this one?

feedback.correct: 口, the mouth -- and it is drawn last, after the piece above it.
feedback.incorrect: 口, the MOUTH. Its three strokes finish the character.

lessons.title: 字 (zì) — a child under a roof
lessons.gloss: a child under a roof — and the word for everything you have been learning

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — the shape and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Write 子, the child — the piece that stands beside 女 in 好.
字 (zì).
Six strokes, and the bottom three are 子, which you have written since the first chapter.
字 (zì) is 子 under a roof. The roof is 宀, a piece rather than a character — three strokes that make a lid:
宀's top dot, pressed down-right.
宀's left side, a short stroke down-left.
宀's horizontal roof, running right and hooking down-left at its end — one stroke 4-6. 子, complete. Its top horizontal turning down-left; its vertical with a left hook; its middle horizontal last.
Five pen lifts.
Roof before child. A covering piece is finished before whatever sits under it, which is the same habit as 日 before the body of 是 and 夕 before 口 in 名 (míng).

And now the meaning, which is the reason this character is worth the effort. 字 zì means character — a written Chinese character. It is the word for the thing you have been learning to make since the first page of this book. The roof-and-child picture is the traditional hook: something raised and kept under shelter.

segments.instruction: 子 alone, then 字 (zì) — the difference is a roof
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: 子 alone, then 字 — the difference is a roof]

segments.instruction: 字 (zì), saying "roof first" before you start
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: 字, saying "roof first" before you start]
[YOU SAY: **zì** — falling]

segments.text: Which goes first, the roof or the child? (The roof.)
Source: Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart; stroke order per the PRC standard Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan (1997).

segments.prompt: This character is the word for the thing you have been writing all along. What does it mean?

feedback.correct: 字 -- a written Chinese character, the unit you have been building since the first page.

lessons.title: 名字 (míngzi) — the word for a name
lessons.gloss: name — literally the characters a name is made of

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Say zǎoshang. Second syllable light and short.
名字 míngzi — name.
Both halves are characters you have just written, and both mean something:
名 míng — name.
字 zì — character, a written unit.

So the word is "name-character", and that is not a stretched hook. A Chinese personal name is a small number of characters, usually two or three, each chosen deliberately for what it means. The word for "name" says what a name is made of.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need — the second syllable goes light again

segments.text: míngzi, not míngzì.

字 (zì) is fourth tone standing alone, and you practised it that way — but in this word it goes neutral, short and light, exactly as 上 did inside 早上. Second syllables do this often, and you now know the signal: no tone mark means no tone.
míng rises; zi rides on the end of it.

segments.source: [REPEAT x2]

segments.instruction: zì alone, falling — then míngzi, with the second syllable light
segments.source: [YOU SAY: **zì** alone, falling — then **míngzi**, with the second syllable light]

segments.instruction: míngzi twice, and say what each of its two halves means
segments.source: [YOU SAY: **míngzi** twice, and say what each of its two halves means]

segments.text: Which syllable of míngzi carries no tone? (The second.)
Source: Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart.

segments.prompt: The word for 'name' is made of two characters. What does the second one mean on its own?

feedback.correct: 字, a written character -- a name is the characters it is made of.
feedback.incorrect: CHARACTER. 名字 is name plus character.

lessons.title: Practice — saying who you are
lessons.gloss: saying who you are, with your own name in it

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Say wǒ shì — low and dipping, then falling.
Two people meet in the morning. The gap in the third line is yours to fill.
A: 早上好 zǎoshang hǎo — good morning. B: 早上好 zǎoshang hǎo — good morning. A: 我是 … wǒ shì … — I am … (your name). B: 我是 … wǒ shì … — I am … (their name). A: 再见 zàijiàn — goodbye.
Say it with your own name in it, out loud. That is the first time this book has asked you for something it could not supply.

blocks.title: What you've built — and one thing deliberately withheld

segments.text: You can now greet by time of day, say who you are, and leave. Every line is built from characters you have written.

One honest gap, and it is worth naming rather than hiding. You have the word for name — 名字 (míngzi) — but not yet the way to ask for someone's. The natural Mandarin question needs a word this book has not given you, and asking it with only the pieces you have would mean teaching you a sentence a speaker would not say. It is coming, and it is worth waiting for.

What 名字 (míngzi) buys you now is real: you can recognise the word when someone else uses it, and you know that a name is characters — which is why a Chinese speaker asked about their name will often tell you which characters it uses.

segments.instruction: wǒ shì, then your own name, three times
segments.source: [YOU SAY: **wǒ shì**, then your own name, three times]

segments.instruction: the whole exchange, taking both parts
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the whole exchange, taking both parts]

segments.instruction: 我是 (wǒ shì), then 名字 (míngzi)
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: 我是, then 名字]

segments.text: Can you yet ask someone else for their name? (Not yet — and the book would rather say so than hand you a sentence nobody says.)
Source: Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart.

segments.prompt: In pinyin, what two words do you put in front of your own name to introduce yourself?

feedback.correct: 我是 -- I am, then your name.
feedback.incorrect: wǒ shì, 我是 -- literally 'I am'.
